articles.title_orig: Russian drone kills 14 at Ukraine train station, but local truce credited to Melania Trump brings some hope
articles.title_zh: Russian drone kills 14 at Ukraine train station, but local truce credited to Melania Trump brings some hope
articles.content_orig:
Kherson, Ukraine — A jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.
A Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, meanwhile, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central city of Kremenchuk, Ukrainian authorities said.
In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children, as Russia continued its deadly attacks on civilians even as a localized ceasefire credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump held in the stricken city of Oleshky.
Humanitarian aid was poised to roll into Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as the limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but the neighboring nations remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
Both sides thanked Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.
"The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported," Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.
"Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded," she said. "This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, per their wishes, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work remained unclear.
Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.
A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents had told her they want to leave the city.
She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine's military.
In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.
"Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn't have under the attacks," she said. "For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop."
The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. "It's a breath of freedom, when you don't look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you're not afraid of dying. It's so great," she said, adding: "It's such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon."
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but President Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelenskyy, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States , and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow's invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.
Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield , the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communications.
Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.
"Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius," Putin said late Wednesday. "We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together."

articles.title_orig: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.title_zh: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.content_orig:
The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.
Xi Jinping , who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China , signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort , but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.
According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.
The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."
Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.
Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and by demanding loyalty . "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.
In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.
Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.
However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.
The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.
Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore , notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.
Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.
"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.
Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.
"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.
This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.
"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader .
For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.
This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018 , which removed term limits for state and party leaders.
Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.
"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."
"He can't go on forever," he added.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.
"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW. "To solve this dilemma, the current leader needs to have both the necessary self-confidence and the readiness to take a step back — just like his predecessors did. But not everyone has that kind of confidence."

articles.title_orig: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
articles.title_zh: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
articles.content_orig:
Google parent Alphabet reported its Q3 financial results on Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company’s stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn’t earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year.
The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story’s publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day.
While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google’s Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That’s about a billion more than analyst guesses.
Google is still making a huge amount of money, but there are several troubling trends emerging. The last few years at the company have been all about AI, with generative technology appearing in products from Gmail to Android. Most notably, Google is shifting to an AI search platform powered by Gemini models.
During the earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler discussed the company’s search volume. This is one of the key metrics by which Google tracks its own performance. In the last quarter, Google saw search grow by 12 percent versus last year. Good for the company, right? Except that’s a much slower rate than previous quarters. Growth in Q2 was 17 percent, and Q1 saw 19 percent growth over 2025. Search revenue was also flat in Q3.
So that’s the first problem, likely driven by more consumers using AI chatbots to find answers. The other issue is that Google’s take on AI search isn’t pulling in revenue like standard web search yet. According to Schindler, each AI Mode query earns less revenue compared to a similar web search—there are fewer ads, and they cost less to run.
While Schindler suggested AI mode revenue was set to increase, he was also careful to control expectations. Advertisers may need time, he said, to understand the value in AI search ads. The company’s research reportedly shows that users find these ads more relevant and helpful than the ones they see in traditional search.
As part of the financial disclosure, Google announced an expansion of ads in AI Mode. If you do decide to dip into Google’s search chatbot, you’ll probably see more contextual advertising. These ads will begin appearing in more international markets soon. In the US, where AI Mode ads were already becoming commonplace, Google will implement multi-turn ads. That means the sponsored links will change continuously as you engage in a back-and-forth with the robot. CEO Sundar Pichai noted that these complex interactions are becoming more common as Google pushes more users toward AI Mode.
Google is not slowing down—it’s only going to accelerate the shift toward more AI. Like last quarter , Google reported negative cash flow in Q3. The loss actually increased from -$5.8 billion to -$9.06 billion, a situation that is directly attributable to Google’s runaway AI spending. Google had capital expenditures of $51.4 billion in Q3 and says it still expects total 2026 spending to be between $195 billion and $205 billion. In 2027, Google is targeting more than $300 billion of AI investment.
Credit:
                                      Google Credit:

          
          Google
To support this continued spending, Google points to its cloud revenue more than doubling over the past year. It’s easy to see why the company is so keen to keep expanding in AI based on that. The company’s AI compute infrastructure doesn’t just power Gemini. Countless AI startups pay to run models on Google’s infrastructure. But even the larger AI firms are using venture cash to do it, and if that funding were to dry up, Google’s cloud revenues could go with it.
While Google’s investments ensure it still turns a profit, the trend of spending more than it earns on products and services (that negative cash flow) could come back to bite it. Search growth is declining, and Google is placing all its eggs in the AI basket. If spending on cloud services in the industry drops or search growth stalls, the company could be looking at a lot more red in its future.

articles.title_orig: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.title_zh: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
CIPP/E, CIPP/US, CIPM, FIP
Senior information governance officer
Beyond Change Advisory, Hong Kong China Network Security Association
In 2023, the fifth anniversary of the EU General Data Protection Regulation's implementation led to widespread reflection on its effectiveness, faults and international influence. The international cascade of regulations that followed the GDPR's introduction bolstered the idea of the Brussels effect, the phenomenon through which regulation within the European market influences global standards.
One of the most prominent examples is China's Personal Information Protection Law , which shares many of the GDPR's fundamental concepts. Effective 1 Nov. 2021, the PIPL now celebrates its fifth anniversary.
Comparable concepts include their respective principles, definitions of personal data and information and the roles and obligations of data handlers, the PIPL's equivalent to the GDPR's "controllers."
While these comparable approaches may make it easier for organizations to harmonize their operations, the two laws are not like-for-like. Among the most notable deviations is the Chinese approach to lawful bases. The PIPL does not contain an equivalent to Europe's "legitimate interests" basis, with consent relied upon far more heavily.
Now that the PIPL has had time to develop, the law's fifth anniversary provides its own opportunity for reflection on guidance and enforcement under the law to date.
Enforcement mainly comes under the remit of the Cyberspace Administration of China, though other authorities also contribute, primarily the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and Ministry of Public Security and certain sectoral regulators.
While landmark cases are handled by the CAC, enforcement actions involving mobile apps are often addressed by different authorities. Civil litigation has also emerged as a means for challenging unlawful processing, with multiple "guiding cases" now identified, providing greater clarity on specific PIPL compliance requirements.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general
articles.content_orig:
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran's navy said a tanker it described as violating maritime restrictions was damaged and caught fire after striking sea mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the vessel unable to continue sailing.
In a statement, the navy said the incident occurred before noon on Thursday as the tanker was sailing through an area designated as prohibited and unsafe by Iran
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a shipping route in the south of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has insisted vessels can only use northern routes it has authorized.
The navy's statement warned that the Strait of Hormuz was closed "to violating vessels that, without coordination and relying on the lies of the U.S. president, intend to pass through prohibited and unsafe areas."
"These uncoordinated transits through high-risk areas have exposed and will continue to expose vessels and their crews to serious dangers," it added.
Qatar has categorically denied allegations of interfering in Israel's elections or funding efforts to influence their outcome, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of launching a disinformation campaign to drag the small Persian Gulf state into domestic Israeli political disputes.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majid al-Ansari said in a statement that Qatar would not be used as a scapegoat for Israeli politicians' failures, insisting that Doha had no involvement in Israel's political competition and would continue its mediation efforts between Iran and the U.S., as well as wider diplomatic engagement and support for the Palestinian people.
His comments come after Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu alleged that Tuesday's national elections were "stolen by Arab parties" and claimed foreign interference in the vote.
Israel's Shin Bet internal security service is investigating possible Qatari and Turkish funding used in an effort to influence the election outcome, according to reports by the Jerusalem Post and Israel's Channel 13.
"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure," al-Ansari said. "The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures."
Iran's navy has carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and approximately 300 operations targeting American interests in various locations during the war, Iranian Army Navy Coordinating Deputy Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said in an interview published Thursday by the official state-run news agency IRNA .
Moghadam claimed the operations involved missiles and drones and said Iran's navy remains operational despite repeated claims by President Trump and other U.S. officials saying it has been destroyed.
"If the Iranian Navy has been destroyed, why have these forces not come closer than 500 or 600 kilometers to the Strait of Hormuz, or closer than 300 kilometers to our maritime borders? There is a force standing in their way, and that force must be the Navy," he said.
Moghadam did not offer any evidence to substantiate his claims.
IRGC spokesperson Brig. Gen. Abolfazl Mohebi challenged U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) to provide independent evidence for its claims of mine-clearing operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Prove your claim of mine-clearing in the Strait of Hormuz with independent evidence, not a statement!" demanded Mohebi in a post on X , adding that "the reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the skies, on land and at sea — not on social media or in America's  media-warfare rooms."
Earlier Thursday the IRGC said three oil tankers had been disabled after striking mines in the strait, and the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center confirmed one vessel in the area was seen on fire.
In late August, President Trump and CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper insisted the primary shipping lanes of the Strait of Hormuz had been demined and were safe for commercial vessels.
In a statement posted online, Cooper said the U.S. military had "meticulously and quietly" cleared mines previously laid by the IRGC.
"Internationally recognized transit routes in the strait are free of Iranian sea mines thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military," he said. "Today, international shipping lanes are open, and momentum is building."
Iran's Houthi allies said Thursday that a Saudi strike on a residential area in Yemen's western Taiz province killed 12 people, as the two sides continued to exchange fire in the reignited Yemeni civil war.
"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement shared by the group's Saba news agency.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis. The Saudis, who back Yemen's government, have engaged in fighting with the Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast and in deadly back-and-forth strikes.
Iran has used some 5,000 agencies to help it slip past the U.S. naval blockade to import hardware, explosives and trucks needed for its drone and missile programs over land, sea and air, according to a report by the Reuters news agency .
The secret network of military agencies has helped Iran usher at least $2 billion in components into the country since 2025, evading Western sanctions and, since earlier this year, the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels.
Some of the agencies are linked to Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), others to business conglomerates run by the country's elite, Reuters said.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, before the U.S. blockade was imposed but with myriad U.S. and international sanctions in place, a single company, MOD 346428, imported large quantities of rocket propellants, explosives and weapons parts crucial for drones and missile production, as well as trucks that can be used as missile launchers. The hardware was brought in from China, Russia and Germany, Reuters reported.
The agencies all use the address of Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in Tehran. Most were established in 2013, when Iran was struggling under international sanctions, the investigation found.
Iran's Intelligence Ministry said Thursday that it had dismantled four alleged terrorist cells and arrested 16 suspects in the central and southern parts of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, while detaining three more individuals accused of gathering and transmitting information about security and defense sites in the country's southeast.
In a statement, the provincial intelligence directorate said the operations were carried out in recent days following public tips and ongoing intelligence and operational surveillance, in cooperation with other provincial security forces. It alleged that the cells were affiliated with terrorist groups linked to the United States and Israel.

articles.title_orig: Germany does not seek decoupling from China, wants fair trade, president says during Beijing visit
articles.title_zh: Germany does not seek decoupling from China, wants fair trade, president says during Beijing visit
articles.content_orig:
Germany does not seek to decouple from China but wants to address trade imbalances through dialogue, the German president said Thursday.
"Our goal as Europeans is clear. We do not want to decouple from China," Frank-Walter Steinmeier told an audience at Peking University during his visit to Beijing.
"On the contrary, we want to ensure that trade continues to be of benefit to both sides ... Partnership only holds if both sides have something to gain. That is why we are seeking solutions through dialogue for the sectors where great imbalances have arisen," Steinmeier said.
Competition between German and Chinese companies is beneficial "but only when it is based on fair rules and a level playing field," he said.
Steinmeier said Germans do not want the world to split into blocs or see a new confrontation between them, warning that such divisions could undermine international security and cause economic losses.
"It is understandable that China wants to protect its economy against external shocks and negative influences. However, China having greater autonomy must not mean conversely that others are increasingly dependent on China and vulnerable to it," he said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Wednesday that Europe does not seek a trade war with China but is determined to defend its industries from unfair practices.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said the EU’s trade deficit with China in 2025 reached €1 billion ($1.12 billion) per day.
The market share of three major German automakers declined in both Europe and China since 2021, while the added value that these manufacturers generated in Europe dropped by 30-45% in the first half of this year compared to 2021-2022.

articles.title_orig: United States and Japan forge missile production alliance to counter China's power
articles.title_zh: United States and Japan forge missile production alliance to counter China's power
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a production facility in Japan to jointly manufacture advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles , according to the Japanese defense chief.
The decision marks the latest step by the two allies to bolster security capabilities amid heightened concerns over China 's growing military assertiveness across Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement during a news conference Wednesday evening in Cebu, a province in the central Philippines .
His remarks followed a bilateral meeting with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual gathering of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
During a session on Thursday, Koizumi highlighted increased Chinese naval presence near southwestern Japan, noting that three Chinese destroyers alongside a coast guard vessel recently passed through the Osumi Strait south of Kyushu into the Pacific Ocean.
He stated that it was the first time his ministry had recorded such a fleet configuration.
Koizumi pointed to the transit as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region," adding that Tokyo will maintain close surveillance of Chinese naval operations while continuing to accelerate its own military buildup in southwestern Japan.
The annual meetings aim to prevent major conflict and deepen regional cooperation, though the U.S., China, and their respective allies frequently exchange criticisms during the proceedings.
The joint manufacturing effort, titled "Operation Supercharge," will establish a final assembly and inspection plant in Japan for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM.
Koizumi emphasized that these missiles are essential for F-35 stealth fighters, which are operated by both the U.S. and Japanese militaries.
Recounting his meeting with Hegseth, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
He added: "We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means."
In a separate meeting with ASEAN defense ministers led by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., Hegseth offered renewed assurances regarding Washington's commitment to regional stability.
Without calling out Beijing by name, Hegseth outlined the U.S. approach.
"The approach we’re taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the defense chiefs, adding it is "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
He emphasized that the position is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners."
Hegseth reassured the Philippines, Washington’s oldest treaty partner in Asia, that the Trump administration will maintain robust deterrence against Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea, a critical trade waterway claimed almost entirely by China.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles pledged that Australian forces, alongside allies like the U.S., would continue upholding international law despite Chinese actions in disputed waters.
Referring to an incident last year where a Chinese J-16 jet released flares near an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance plane, Marles said: "That doesn’t deter us from doing what we need to do and that’s essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific."
He added: "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
Territorial claims in the South China Sea remain contested among the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan, with frequent standoffs involving Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval vessels.
Washington maintains that it is bound by treaty to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships, or aircraft come under armed attack. Separately, Tokyo and Beijing remain locked in a maritime dispute over Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea.

articles.title_orig: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.title_zh: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.content_orig:
Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least three people and injuring five others, officials said.
A section of the rock formation — known as a fairy chimney — tumbled in Cappadocia’s Goreme region, prompting authorities to deploy medical and rescue teams.
Gov. Huseyin Kok said recent heavy rains likely caused the collapse, which occurred near a parking lot at an entrance to the site.
He said rescue teams were continuing to search for other people who may be trapped under the debris.
“We hope that there are no other casualties,” the governor said. “We are deeply saddened.”
Kok said two of the three dead were Turkish nationals. He did not provide information on the third victim.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation was launched into the incident.
HaberTurk news channel showed heavy machinery removing chunks of rock from the foot of the formation.
Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site famed for its distinctive rock formations and ancient underground cities. It is one of the country’s most visited tourism locations.
The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day holiday, when the area would have been crowded with visitors.

articles.title_orig: DoorDash stock pops, Instacart falls after companies announce $17 billion acquisition deal
articles.title_zh: DoorDash stock pops, Instacart falls after companies announce $17 billion acquisition deal
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
DoorDash ( DASH ) announced plans to acquire hyperlocal grocery delivery provider Instacart ( CART ) on Thursday morning in a deal valued at $17 billion.
DoorDash, which is primarily known for its restaurant food delivery business, will pay $65 per Instacart share, a 26% premium over the stock's Oct. 22 closing price. The transaction includes 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both. Instacart's board of directors unanimously approved the deal, according to a press release.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the release. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
DoorDash stock popped over 5%, while Instacart stock fell 1.5%.
The acquisition comes as Walmart ( WMT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) have been taking share of the grocery delivery market, especially for same-day and one-hour delivery.
Prior to the announcement, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian said the combination of Instacart and DoorDash could "potentially prove to be a competitive differentiation."
"A combination of strong restaurant delivery plus a marketplace including various grocers from Instacart can be a critical combination against Walmart and Amazon in particular, who continue to push in this market as well," Arounian said.
Walmart currently holds a roughly 30.9% share of the online grocery market, ahead of Amazon at roughly 23.6%, per Wedbush.
For customers worried about what the Instacart acquisition means for prices, the company said shoppers will now get two memberships for the price of one and more choices.
"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," the release said.
For local business owners, the company said this would allow them more ways to earn.

articles.title_orig: Russian drone strike kills 14 on Ukrainian rail platform
articles.title_zh: Russian drone strike kills 14 on Ukrainian rail platform
articles.content_orig:
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole in a platform that is strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal that was struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Moscow, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 25 others, including four children, were injured, he added.
A day of mourning has been declared for Chernihiv and Dnipro on Friday.
In the city of Kremenchuk, in the central Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a Russian drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said.
The latest Russian strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity for years.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The two-day event is attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real, and attacks on Ukraine's train infrastructure have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency.
Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in the capital Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq 100 Falls 1.5% as AI Trade Shows New Cracks: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq 100 Falls 1.5% as AI Trade Shows New Cracks: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Steve Eisman of "The Big Short" fame thinks the artificial intelligence trade is near a "tipping point," but he's not ready to outright bet against it yet.
"I've gotten much more conservative in my own portfolio. We have shorted against the box a whole bunch of our positions, so that our risk is much, much, much lower. But I'm not, like, net short any," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday.
Eisman's primary concern pertains to the frontier algorithm models, which are exploiting a climate of fear around their technologies, he believes, in order to set up a competitive regulatory moat against more cost-efficient products and to obscure some faltering fundamentals. Bigwigs in the tech industry have issued similar warnings .
Anthropic left its latest revenue figures blank in its initial IPO filing, but Eisman believes they will show a significant deceleration from the prior quarter. Other figures in the report point to capital efficiency issue, he said.
The ratio of revenue-to-equipment-expense was 2.08 in the second quarter and 1.7 in the third, marking a significant change in trajectory, Eisman said, citing an analysis he'd been given.
Yet, Eisman said he was scared to make a definitive bet against the AI trade because of how intertwined it is with the market as a whole, calling it "impossible" for the technology sector to be siloed away from the broader equity market and the rest of the economy.
"So much of the market is on the other side, and it's still reading tea leaves. I think we're getting closer. I think the numbers from Google scared people," he said.
Alphabet's stock tanked after reporting earnings on Wednesday, following a big pullback in its core advertising business as AI queries supplant internet search across its various products.
Google executives said Wednesday they were running experiments to figure out what to do about it.
"It's worth noting the strong growth in AI mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we are seeing in AI mode," Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said. "Our ad experiments have shown promising results."
Portions of Anthropic's recently filed S-1 struck Eisman as "extremely negative" in light of the fact that it didn't contain many metrics for the upcoming quarter that would give a clearer picture of the company's financial situation.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft’s AI future has fewer jobs
articles.title_zh: Microsoft’s AI future has fewer jobs
articles.content_orig:
It’s also time to name the next Elder Scrolls game, and Xbox’s architect of Forza Motorsport is leaving.
It’s also time to name the next Elder Scrolls game, and Xbox’s architect of Forza Motorsport is leaving.
To anyone listening closely to what Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been saying over the past couple of years, this week felt like the clearest sign yet that AI is about to fundamentally change the size of Microsoft’s workforce. Microsoft is now offering voluntary buyouts to around 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada, and India.
It’s the first time the company has presented such an offer to so many employees, expanding greatly upon the retirement offer that was limited to around 9,000 employees earlier this year. It’s all part of an ongoing effort to avoid reducing investment in AI infrastructure by lowering Microsoft’s operating costs and headcount.
“Our total people costs will go down, our cost per head will go up, and my GPU per researcher will go up,” Nadella said on a podcast almost two years ago, responding to a question about AI’s impact on headcount. That’s a financial way of saying Microsoft will have fewer people, but it will offer higher salaries and more tools and AI power to those who remain.
It also helps explain the continued layoffs we’ve seen at Microsoft over the past couple of years. Microsoft has been performing layoffs regularly over the past decade, but over the past couple of years, the layoffs and executive departures have been significant.
These aren’t the annual layoffs of old; they’re now happening every few months. This week’s voluntary exit offer arrived just months after Microsoft laid off 4,800 employees , cuts that impacted its Xbox and commercial sales teams the most.
For the first time in a decade, Microsoft’s overall headcount has also gone down year over year . Microsoft now employs around 223,000 people as of June 30th, 5,000 fewer than the 228,000 people it employed in 2025. Microsoft laid off 4 percent of its workforce in July last year, and it’s now offering voluntary buyout offers to around a quarter of its employees.
More than 30 percent of the 9,000 eligible employees accepted a retirement offer earlier this year, but that number will likely be far less for the company’s latest Voluntary Exit Offer. That’s largely because, according to sources familiar, the offer is practically the same as regular severance terms at Microsoft — cash based on time at the company, accelerated stock vesting, some additional subsidized health coverage, and several months of career services.
But what makes this unusual is the scale of the amount of employees who have been offered this exit. Even if only 5 percent accept the offer, that’s still 3,000 employees. I understand eligible employees have until December to decide, so we won’t know the impact of this offer for a while yet. With rumors of more layoffs in November and January, the amount of employees who do accept will surely inform Microsoft’s numbers for its next round of cuts.
There are some, both inside and outside the company, who think Microsoft needs these cuts. “Microsoft needs fewer people,” says Merill Fernando , a former Microsoft Entra product manager. “I’ve been on the inside. I’ve seen how things get built. Lots of small orgs. Layers on layers. Silos everywhere.”
Fernando paints a picture of a Microsoft where every organization “had its own priorities and its own decision makers,” so it’s hard to get the company to do anything collectively. It sounds a little like the meme where each organization in Microsoft is pointing guns at each other, competing instead of collaborating.
Nadella even addressed that meme last year in a podcast with Stripe co-founder John Collison , acknowledging that the comic has defined Microsoft’s cultural narrative “more so than reality,” but that it had signaled some very real tensions inside the company. “In some sense, some of these divisional tensions are real issues that need to have tension. Social cohesion is not a goal, winning in the marketplace is a goal,” said Nadella.
The question now is whether Nadella can reshape Microsoft for the AI era without undoing the cultural transformation that helped define his leadership. A company that has shifted to be built around empathy is now asking its employees to reckon with an AI future that could make many of their jobs unnecessary. How Nadella handles that transition will define his legacy as much as the growth and success he’s achieved over the past decade.
A few weeks ago I started hearing from Xbox employees that Dan Greenawalt , the longtime creative force behind Forza Motorsport , is leaving after almost 27 years. Greenawalt is departing as the head of Turn 10 Studios, the Forza Motorsport creator that merged with Forza Horizon developer Playground Games.
Playground Games studio head Trevor Williams revealed the news in a recent internal memo, seen by Notepad . “Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft,” says Williams. Greenawalt will stay on as an adviser to Williams and the newly appointed Playground Games chief operating officer, Michel Bastien, “while he transitions to his next phase.” Here’s part of Williams’ memo about Greenawalt:
It’s hard to overstate Dan’s impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original XBOX in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow – and so much more – we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.
Microsoft revealed last month that it was merging its two Forza developers into a single studio as part of a massive restructuring of Xbox . Both Playground Games and Turn 10 Studios have merged into just Playground Games. The studio now has two locations: Playground Games Leamington Spa and Playground Games Redmond.
With Greenawalt retiring and Turn 10 merged into Playground Games, it’s not clear if we’ll ever see Microsoft return to Forza Motorsport . More than 70 people at Turn 10 Studios were laid off last year , in a move that hit the vast majority of the studio. Over the past year, Turn 10 Studios has essentially been maintaining Forza Motorsport , and now the remaining employees have moved to Playground Games to work on Forza Horizon and Fable .
It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda officially announced the existence of the sixth game in its Elder Scrolls series. While there have been some debates around platform exclusivity for The Elder Scrolls VI , we’ve heard very little detail about the game that Bethesda has been working on all this time.
Sources familiar with Bethesda’s plans tell me that the Xbox-owned publisher is about to announce that the next Elder Scrolls game will officially be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel . The announcement could come as soon as next month, during a period that will mark 15 years since The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released.
Bethesda has been showing off Sentinel gameplay in recent months, I’m told. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma got a live playthrough of Sentinel in August, and she praised the scale of the game and said “the story is even greater.”
While I’m only expecting a name reveal next month and nothing more, I’ve been hearing some additional details about the game. If you want to totally avoid spoilers about the game, then don’t read the next paragraph.
I understand that Sentinel will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online . Sentinel will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts.
I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here,

articles.title_orig: Nvidia responds to report Jensen Huang was target of Chinese asset, says diversion allegations were 'investigated and debunked'
articles.title_zh: Nvidia responds to report Jensen Huang was target of Chinese asset, says diversion allegations were 'investigated and debunked'
articles.content_orig:
An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.
The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
"The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang.
"We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology.
As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure.
Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed.
"Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.

The delightfully devious stealth platformer Deathmaster has its story trailer revealed today. The story centers around Vinheek, a powerless Skaven prisoner when we first meet him, who has plans for greatness. Vihneek is freed by Skiteek, a fellow assassin from Clan Skrell – but Vihneek’s savior is ultimately his new captor. articles.title_orig: Von der Leyen touts ‘associate member’ status for Canada over objections of EU capitals
articles.title_zh: Von der Leyen touts ‘associate member’ status for Canada over objections of EU capitals
articles.content_orig:
MONTREAL, Canada — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday she aims to bring EU-Canada relations to the “highest level possible,” touting potential associate member status in the bloc for Ottawa despite capitals having rejected the term a day earlier.
Von der Leyen’s overture comes on the eve of a landmark EU-Canada summit in Montreal where she and Prime Minister Mark Carney are due to announce plans for deeper cooperation against a backdrop of rising autocracy globally and unpredictable relations with U.S. President Donald Trump.
“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said in a speech hosted by the C.D. Howe Institute. “This is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.”
No sooner had von der Leyen finished speaking than German Chancellor Friedrich Merz issued a statement saying that the EU and Canada were establishing an “Alliance for the Future” — without mentioning the associate member status. Germany has led the opposition to using the term, according to EU diplomats.
“We are fighting each other about a few words which von der Leyen pulled out of thin air,” one of those EU diplomats told POLITICO on Wednesday. “It’s a bit silly while we should have ambition and focus on other things. This is not our proudest moment.”
In a speech hours later on the sidelines of the summit, European Council President António Costa sought to bridge the divide by playing down the importance of the term.
“Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an Alliance for the Future of Europe,” he said in a nod to Merz’s statement and using the term preferred by Carney to describe the relationship.
“President von der Leyen has even put forward the bold idea of making Canada an ‘associate member’ of the European Union,” he said, noting “I share her ambition.”
“Whether that ends up being the term or not, one thing is clear: our partnership will be the closest, deepest and most unique of its kind,” he added.
The Commission president said in her speech that talks about associate membership would focus on deeper cooperation across AI, climate and energy policy, as well as bolstering shared work between the European Commission and the Canadian government as well as “Parliament to Parliament” and “Court to Court,” a reference to the European Court of Justice and Canada’s Supreme Court.
Such a status, she said, would be open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe, who are ready to open a new frontier together — and to chart the course together, to think beyond the terms of our partnership today, toward the most ambitious vision we can build.”
Von der Leyen’s use of the term associate membership — which she first mentioned in September — is likely to rub some EU capitals the wrong way after a group of countries led by Germany objected to including a reference to the term in a joint EU-Canada statement that was seen by POLITICO and is due to be published on Friday.
After days of talks, EU countries opted for softer language to describe the two sides’ future relations, including the “Alliance for the Future” — the term used by the Canadian side — as well as an “even closer association ... short of full membership.”
EU diplomats have told POLITICO that while capitals support the broader aim of closer ties with Canada, they are wary of offering a status that has never been proposed before and whose legal contours remain undefined. Berlin had previously floated associate member status for Ukraine, including specific privileges such as observer status in the European Commission, but that effort was rejected.
Reacting to reports that EU countries would drop the “associate member” term, Carney said on Tuesday: “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.”
Both Carney and von der Leyen have cast this week’s summit as part of a broader effort to deepen ties at a time when both Ottawa and Brussels have clashed with the Trump administration, with von der Leyen warning in her speech about “deeper decay in the international order.”
“Alliances and assumptions that have enabled our prosperity and security are changing rapidly, and each nation or region is looking at how to secure its own interests and its own independence,” she said. “We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old-world order.”
This story has been updated. Camille Gijs contributed reporting from Brussels.

articles.title_orig: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
articles.title_zh: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
articles.content_orig:
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.
DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.
Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.
"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.
"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.
For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's  grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.
He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".
The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.
Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.
"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.
In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.
DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.
The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.
New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."
"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

articles.title_orig: Iran’s hidden web of military agencies is slipping hardware past the US blockade
articles.title_zh: Iran’s hidden web of military agencies is slipping hardware past the US blockade
articles.content_orig:
Iran has used a secret network of more than 5,000 military agencies to import at least $2 billion worth of equipment, explosives and heavy-duty trucks since January 2025, bypassing Western sanctions and the US naval blockade, a Reuters investigation published on Thursday found.
One agency alone, identified as MOD 346428, imported $2.3 billion in military-related goods between January 2025 and June 2026, according to shipping records examined by Reuters.
The shipments included rocket fuel ingredients, explosives, aircraft parts, industrial machinery and hundreds of heavy-duty trucks that could be adapted for military use, with goods recorded as originating in China, Russia, Germany and other countries.
The findings provide details of how Iran has continued to obtain materials used in missile and drone production during the US-Israeli war, which began in February, despite attacks on its weapons production facilities.
Thousands of agencies linked to defense ministry
Reuters identified more than 5,000 agencies whose names begin with MOD, referring to Iran's Ministry of Defense, and which share the Tehran address of the Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics.
Although their registration records list February 11, 1979, as their founding date, most were established in 2013, when Iran was facing severe economic sanctions, the investigation found.
Reuters and Israeli-American risk consultancy 240 Analytics traced the agencies through Iranian banking records, corporate filings and shipping documents, including around 19,000 import records.
Some entities were linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and large Iranian foundations known as bonyads.
The agencies use intermediaries and overseas companies to purchase goods with proceeds from oil sales that bypass sanctions, according to the investigation.
In 97% of the shipments reviewed, transactions were recorded as settled "without currency transfer," allowing purchases to be made using funds held outside Iran.
Banking records also showed that 36 agencies held about $1.2 billion in foreign currency deposits at the end of 2024, while the wider network held around $1.8 billion in local currency, Reuters reported.
The news agency said it found no evidence that the numbered agencies identified in the documents had been individually sanctioned by Western governments.
Missile materials and hundreds of trucks imported
The investigation found that Iran continued importing materials that could be used in missiles and drones after the war began on February 28.
In the first six months of 2026, deliveries included detonators, explosives, aircraft engine components and rocket fuel ingredients.
In February, shortly before the war, Iran imported 93 metric tons of Chinese titanium and hundreds of tons of chemicals that could be used in rocket propellants and explosives, according to customs records.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, MOD 346428 also imported 435 Iveco trucks, some of which matched models used as disguised mobile missile launchers, Reuters reported.
The same agency imported thousands of Toyota Hilux and Land Cruiser vehicles, as well as Toyota Tundra trucks, models that Iranian forces have used for military purposes.
The investigation also traced imports of chemicals to the port of Bandar Abbas, where an explosion in April 2025 killed at least 70 people and injured more than 1,200.
Reuters said it could not determine whether chemicals in one of the shipments it identified were responsible for the explosion.
It also could not establish that all imported goods were intended for weapons production, noting that many materials and machines have both civilian and military uses.
Imports continued during war and blockade
The materials entered Iran through several routes, including cargo vessels crossing the Caspian Sea from Russia, trucks traveling from Central Asia and freight aircraft arriving from China, Reuters reported.
Monthly imports by the identified military agency fell by 47% to $54 million in March, shortly after the war began, but recovered to $77 million by May.
The investigation identified five shipments of Russian detonators worth $7.6 million since January 2025, including a $1.9 million delivery in June 2026.
Since the war began, $27 million worth of goods purchased by Iran's military were recorded as originating in the United Arab Emirates, mostly arriving by sea.
The Reuters data also listed hundreds of millions of dollars in trucks, aircraft components and electronics as coming from Germany and other European Union countries.
Reuters cautioned that some customs records identified shipments only through product codes and declared countries of origin, which it could not always independently verify.
Western companies and governments respond
China's Foreign Ministry told Reuters it was unaware of the reported shipments and rejected attempts to link Beijing to the regional conflict.
"We firmly oppose attempts to maliciously link regional hostilities to China or smear China's reputation," the ministry said.
Italian truck manufacturer Iveco said it had safeguards to prevent its vehicles from reaching prohibited users and destinations but could not control products resold by third parties.
Toyota said it did not conduct business in Iran and had no knowledge of the purchases described in the investigation.
The European Union said it was examining information about Iran's efforts to strengthen its missile and drone programs.
A US Treasury spokesperson said Washington had cut off Iran's economic lifelines and would continue enforcing sanctions.
"While the regime may continue its desperate attempts to evade our powerful sanctions, fund its military and weapons programs, and access foreign currency, we are always 10 steps ahead," the spokesperson said.
Iranian government bodies and companies contacted by Reuters, including the country's presidency and its UN delegation in Geneva, did not respond to requests for comment.
The newspaper said a change in Israeli leadership would not necessarily reduce military threats against Iran but could weaken the political and diplomatic networks Netanyahu has built during his years in power.
"Ultimately, Netanyahu's departure is in Iran's interest, not because his successor would necessarily adopt a friendly approach, but because removing one of the main architects of the confrontation with Iran would reduce the accumulated political and diplomatic capacity behind it," Khorasan wrote.
The assessment came after Israel's parliamentary election on Tuesday produced no clear winner, leaving Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot , seeking support to form a government.
With nearly 86% of votes counted on Wednesday, Israeli broadcasters projected Netanyahu's right-wing bloc would secure 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for Eisenkot's opposition bloc and 19 for Arab-led parties.
Neither main bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a majority, leaving the outcome dependent on coalition negotiations.
Netanyahu's experience seen as key factor
Khorasan said Israeli political groups shared many positions on security matters despite their differences and that Eisenkot, a former military chief, was not opposed to confrontation with Iran.
It argued, however, that Netanyahu had built political and diplomatic networks over many years that a successor could find difficult to replace.
"Netanyahu is not merely a prime minister," the newspaper wrote, adding that he had developed extensive political, regional and international connections and considerable experience influencing US decision-making.
The newspaper said Netanyahu knew how to make Iran a central issue in Washington's foreign policy and connect security developments with political opportunities.
"Removing such a figure from the top of power, even if the basic structure of Israeli policy remains unchanged, means losing part of this accumulated capacity," it said.

articles.title_orig: Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site
articles.title_zh: Finland launches criminal investigation into Google’s clearing of forest for datacentre site
articles.content_orig:
Authorities allege company may have breached Finnish environmental laws by forgoing required impact assessment
‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
Finnish ⁠police have launched a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of the country’s environmental ⁠laws ​at the site of a planned Google datacentre in rural northern Finland .
Authorities allege that Tuike Finland, a Google subsidiary, cleared and drained 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest at the planned site in Muhos before environmental impact assessments required by Finnish law had been completed.
Like other Nordic countries, Finland is attractive to tech companies seeking to build datacentres because of its relative geopolitical stability and abundance of land, but also because its cool climate should allow them to cut energy costs.
“Based on preliminary information, there have been ambiguities and ‌shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the construction site of Tuike Finland ​Oy’s datacentre project,” Finnish police said in a statement on Thursday.
“The criminal investigation will examine, among other things, circumstances related to these issues,” they added.
Finnish authorities are considering applications for a total of 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, including a €13bn (£11bn) artificial intelligence infrastructure project by Google that the US company has called its largest ‌investment in Europe.
Earlier this month Finnish authorities ordered Google to suspend work at two sites – Muhos and Otanmäki, about 100km to the south-east – after the company failed to complete environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land.
The Supervisory ⁠Agency, which oversees environmental permits and assessments, told Google to halt “preparatory ​measures altering the environment”. Campaigners estimate 250,000 trees have been felled at Muhos and 150,000 at Otanmäki.
Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings, but argued that the company had acted according to “the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.
The Finnish government has encouraged the projects. In September, when Google’s plans were announced, the prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and the deal would “deliver lasting benefits”.
But the revelations over Google’s alleged misconduct have sparked a national debate over what datacentre deals mean for communities, the environment and energy prices. The issue could impact parliamentary elections due in April.
More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and compensation for environmental damage. Experts say datacentres bring a limited number of local jobs, and benefits on a national level are minimal.
“Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” said Jussi Kangasharju, professor of computer science at University of Helsinki. “They are international companies serving international customers. Datacentres ultimately have little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”

articles.title_orig: Stanley Druckenmiller backs push to bring risky crypto-style bets to Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Stanley Druckenmiller backs push to bring risky crypto-style bets to Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
The post appeared seemingly out of nowhere. Stanley Druckenmiller, the legendary hedge fund manager who brought the Bank of England to its knees in the 1990s, and whose annual returns are the envy of Wall Street, posted a simple message on an otherwise sparse X feed announcing his involvement with a new type of decentralized exchange. The post caused bedlam on social media and moved shares of a leading crypto treasury company and its token.
TradeXYZ, the primary developer of perpetual futures, or "perps" markets, on exchange Hyperliquid, announced a partnership Thursday with Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) to bring its popular perpetual futures onshore into the U.S.
Shortly after the two said they are seeking regulatory approvals, Druckenmiller said on X that he is "excited to be an investor in trade(xyz)," and that he is "looking forward to to using their innovative product to enhance my investment process." Representatives for Druckenmiller confirmed the statement to the Financial Times .
Options traders pounced on the closest publicly-traded play to the news: Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR) , the company that invests in the HYPE crypto token that powers the Hyperliquid exchange.
More than 111,000 options traded on Hyperliquid Strategies Thursday, more than six times the 30-day average, as underlying shares surged 19% to the highest in three weeks. The flows leaned bullish, with almost 86,000 calls and under 27,000 puts trading. Almost four times as many calls were likely initiated by buyers than puts, and of the top 10 trades, only one involved put-buying, Cboe LiveVol dat show.
"We are thrilled to see ICE partnering with Trade.XYZ to bring the markets and liquidity of Hyperliquid to American investors," David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies, said in a text. "ICE is a cornerstone of traditional finance and the ideal partner."
Schamis added that the deal shows demand for perp-futures trading and is a step forward toward regulated trading of the asset class.
In August, President Donald Trump said in a surprise comment to reporters that regulators were working to bring the exchange onshore.
The most popular trades by volume in PURR were selling the 13-strike put expiring Dec. 18, and buying the 13-strike call expiring Nov. 6. Taken together, the two resemble a "risk reversal" strategy, a bullish trade looking for a short-term continuation of the rally, paired with long-term confidence the stock won't be below $13 by year-end.

articles.title_zh: iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when to expect new iPhone features
articles.content_orig:
Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages , Siri AI , and Photos , plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update.
If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.
For example, iOS 27.2 launched this week right around the same time as Apple’s previous releases in years past.
The only difference is that normally we would have expected iOS 27.1 in the last week of October rather than 27.2. But due to Apple making iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo , all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.
That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.
iOS 27.3 is expected to arrive in beta within the next few days—Monday, November 2 is likely.
As for the public launch, here’s what past years have shown for comparable x.2 updates:
Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release in mid-December .
Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.
As for new iPhone features in iOS 27.3, we’ll know a lot more after the beta arrives. So far though, at a minimum we’re expecting the additional Siri AI languages Apple announced this week, plus the return of the all-new Health app .
