articles.title_orig: 'We Did This To Support The BDS Boycott' - Two Xbox Games Delisted As Celeste Developer Issues Statement
articles.title_zh: 'We Did This To Support The BDS Boycott' - Two Xbox Games Delisted As Celeste Developer Issues Statement
articles.content_orig:
Celeste and TowerFall have been delisted from Xbox, as the developer has chosen to boycott Microsoft for its involvement and investments with the Israeli government.
Developer Maddy Thorson, the mind behind Celeste and TowerFall, confirmed on Bluesky that her team had removed the games from Xbox. They are no longer available to purchase on the platform, which caught some fans by surprise. Thorson stated that she made the decision to remove the titles in support of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement, which describes itself as a “Palestinian-led movement for freedom, justice and equality.” IGN has asked Microsoft for comment on the situation.
The movement targets companies that are involved with or invested in the Israeli government amidst the ongoing conflict between Israel and Palestine. Celeste and TowerFall are not the first games to drop Xbox as a result of this movement, either. Earlier this fall, the beloved co-op adventure game, Big Walk, chose not to release on Xbox and cited the boycott as its reason . The team noted that, should Microsoft divest from its Israeli ties and be removed from the list of BDS targets, Big Walk would be brought to Xbox.
"We have made the decision not to release Big Walk on Xbox, in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement’s call to boycott Microsoft, and their designation of Microsoft Games (and Xbox) as a priority boycott target," said Big Walk developer House House at the time. "If you need help understanding our motives, we would recommend reading about why Microsoft is a BDS priority target, the successes this kind of pressure has already had on Microsoft, and especially, watching this great introductory piece by People Make Games ."
Celeste and TowerFall have both been out for some time, with the latter having been released in 2013 and the former in 2018. Both games remain available for purchase on PlayStation, PC, and Switch.

articles.content_orig:
While the 2025 reveal of the Switch 2 came with many surprises, none were as unexpected as The Duskbloods . It's a Switch 2 exclusive, multiplayer-only title from FromSoftware, the developer behind games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring; in other words, not your typical Nintendo game. While The Duskbloods was originally scheduled to launch sometime this year, today the developer announced it's pushing the game's launch to 2027.
According to a post on The Duskbloods' X account , the main reason for the delay was balance-related. Here's the full statement:
While development of "The Duskbloods" is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027. We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support. During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing.
We attended a hands-on preview session earlier this year and came away very positive, and sentiment was similar following the game's closed network test ( that is, when the servers were working properly ). It's not surprising that the devs have changes in mind following so much public feedback, though it is a little surprising that it will take until sometime next year for those adjustments to be complete.
To tide you over until the game's launch, check out our in-depth preview impressions or watch the video above to hear our live commentary over gameplay footage. You can also hear us discuss the game on our podcast, The Game Informer Show .

articles.title_zh: Fairy chimney rockfall kills two at Turkey's Cappadocia tourist attraction after heavy rain
articles.content_orig:
Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least three people and injuring five others, officials said.
A section of the rock formation — known as a fairy chimney — tumbled in Cappadocia’s Goreme region, prompting authorities to deploy medical and rescue teams.
Gov. Huseyin Kok said recent heavy rains likely caused the collapse, which occurred near a parking lot at an entrance to the site.
He said rescue teams were continuing to search for other people who may be trapped under the debris.
“We hope that there are no other casualties,” the governor said. “We are deeply saddened.”
Kok said two of the three dead were Turkish nationals. He did not provide information on the third victim.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation was launched into the incident.
HaberTurk news channel showed heavy machinery removing chunks of rock from the foot of the formation.
Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site famed for its distinctive rock formations and ancient underground cities. It is one of the country’s most visited tourism locations.
The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day holiday, when the area would have been crowded with visitors.

articles.title_orig: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge rose in September as third-quarter GDP beats expectations
articles.title_zh: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge rose in September as third-quarter GDP beats expectations
articles.content_orig:
The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below.
Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.
While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter.
GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter.
Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%.
The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move.
"The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do.
A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.
Stock market future s were negative following the releases while Treasury yields also fell.
"Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The economy was thought to have been a lost cause during much of the current Administration's time in office, but real GDP has bounced back above a 3 percent run rate in Q3 2026 for the first time in a year."
Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment from the artificial intelligence build-out, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products.
Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter.
There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter.
September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%.
At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

On his 368th day without a job, Dia Harris woke at 8:30, slipped a coffee pod into his Keurig and checked his iPad to see how many more rejections had come in overnight.
There were two automated messages from “Meta Careers,” thanking him for applying to be a program manager. “Our recruiting team will contact you if your qualifications are a strong match,” Harris read. By his count, those were the 560th and 561st roles he’d sought since getting fired from the federal government.

articles.title_orig: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
articles.title_zh: Hong Kong leader apologizes for deadly fire that tested Beijing’s grip on city
articles.content_orig:
Blaze was world’s deadliest residential fire since 1980, but some survivors and bereaved families say justice has yet to be served
Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.
The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.
Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.
Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.
Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.
Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.
The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.
Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.
Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.
“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.
But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.
Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.
She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.
Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism than addressing the causes of the disaster.
Since a national security law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.
In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.
China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.
On Thursday Lee promised that “similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.
Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.
Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.
The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”

articles.title_orig: Russia says war 'must continue' after Ukraine's 'massive' drone attack on Moscow
articles.title_zh: Russia says war 'must continue' after Ukraine's 'massive' drone attack on Moscow
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli national security expert warns a single missile launch could spark rapid escalation amid major military drills.
The Israeli military launched large-scale domestic military exercises on Sunday to counter surprise border infiltrations and ground raids across northern and central Israel, mobilizing multiple divisions and air assets amid rising regional tensions.
The drills, set to continue over 48 hours, came as an Israeli security expert invoked the 1973 Yom Kippur War, when Egypt and Syria used exercises to disguise preparations for a surprise attack, warning that escalating tensions in the region could in fact trigger what he described as a "dangerous miscalculation."
The large-scale maneuvers, the IDF said, involve the Northern Command’s 210th Division, the West Bank Division, and the Central Command’s 98th and 96th divisions, alongside the Israeli Air Force.
IRAN TARGETS US WITH PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE CAMPAIGN TO MANIPULATE AMERICANS, EMBARRASS TRUMP: EXPERTS
The military exercise is not against Iran directly but against Iran's proxies and allies at the border of Israel, analysts said. ( Jalaa MAREY / AFP via Getty Images)
The exercise, scheduled just ahead of Israel's elections Oct. 27, aims to "maintain the forces’ alertness and readiness, strengthen the ability to defend communities, and make full use of aerial capabilities for defense in the area," according to the IDF.
On Friday, the IDF said troops would practice "a variety of scenarios, including a surprise attack and infiltration into Israeli territory by air and land," incorporating lessons learned from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel.
"This exercise is mostly about non-state actors with or without Iranian support," Israeli national security analyst Dr. Ehud Eilam told Fox News Digital.
"It's aimed at those in Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan who might try to infiltrate into Israel or send ground raids. Some are supported by Iran; others are not. It could be planned by Iran or be a local initiative."
NETANYAHU PRAISES TRUMP'S 'WICKED SENSE OF HUMOR,' DEFENDS IRONCLAD ALLIANCE AHEAD OF HISTORIC ISRAEL VOTE
Iranian missiles are seen targeting Israel during the recent conflict. (Pool via WANA/Reuters)
"This is a massive exercise, the biggest one in recent years, aimed at protecting the borders," the former Israeli Ministry of Defense researcher added.
"It's all about making sure that the election day on October 27 will run smoothly. It's also a message to Iran and others: don't try to provoke us during election day, so nothing will be disrupted."
The Israeli drills followed a show of force by Tehran days earlier, during which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired roughly 30 ballistic missiles across two distinct weapon classes, according to reports .
That live-fire display highlighted Iranian strike capabilities and sparked renewed alerts about commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and prompted the Israeli military to heighten its alert level while maintaining maximum readiness for a targeted strike against Iran.
TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME
The IDF is practicing surprise attack and infiltration scenarios using lessons from the Oct. 7, 2023, assault. (Amir Levy/Getty Images)
During a visit to the IDF's Central Command on Wednesday, Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir warned that the risk of escalation was growing.
"Given the numerous warnings across all fronts and the sensitivity of the current period, the potential for escalation has increased ," Zamir said.
"To ensure better operational control on the ground, we have reinforced our troop deployments across all sectors, including moving the 98th Division into the area to strengthen security and stability."
"Part of mutual deterrence: a few days ago, Iran had their own pretty big exercise, and that was actually more intimidating as far as Israel is concerned because they launched missiles and prepared for a war with Israel," Eilam said.
"This exercise on Sunday and Monday is against Iran's proxies and allies at the border of Israel."
Sunday’s Israeli drill also followed an Oct. 19 mission in which Israeli fighter jets and aerial refueling tankers flew 800 miles across Syrian and Iraqi airspace to Iran’s border.
FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY
An Israeli fighter jet takes off for strikes in Tehran. (IDF)
Washington was notified in advance and viewed the maneuver as a non-kinetic show of force following the postponement of a broader strike package earlier in the month.
Despite the deterrence signals, Eilam warned that large-scale military exercises carry the "risk of miscalculation" and particularly when troop movements could be mistaken for preparations for an attack.
"During the Cold War, every time the Soviet Union or NATO carried out a major drill, having so many troops in the field meant they might attack if that was the intention," Eilam said.
He pointed to the 1973 Yom Kippur War , when Egypt and Syria used military exercises to help conceal troop buildups along Israel's borders.
Israeli intelligence largely dismissed the movements as routine drills, allowing the two countries to achieve strategic surprise when they launched a coordinated, two-front attack on Yom Kippur.
TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE
Military personnel perform during a military parade in Damascus, Syria, Dec. 8, 2025. (Khalil Ashawi/Reuters)
"The classic example in Israel is 1973, when Egypt and Syria conducted a major exercise just before the war that turned into the actual attack," the analyst said.
"Israel and Iran are now watching each other very closely and both sides suspect the other might strike first," Eilam added before stating that there is the chance of what they call "miscalculation — that each side suspects the other and strikes first by mistake."
"It's all about sending messages to each other."
"It remains uncertain whether there will eventually be an Israeli attack on Iran because it depends on U.S. authorization," Eilam concluded.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Right now, both sides are signaling: 'We are ready, don't mess with us, but we don't want to start a war right now.'"
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Zwift Plus Explained: Zwift Video Routes & Zwift Coach Hands-On
articles.title_zh: Zwift Plus Explained: Zwift Video Routes & Zwift Coach Hands-On
articles.content_orig:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy
(Photo: Zwift/Corie Spruill)
Video routes mean more routes Lots of new badges to chase Quality machine learning based structured training system Workouts use group rides and RoboPacers instead of just ERG mode Immediate post-ride coach analysis on pacing and fatigue
Requires an upgraded Zwift Plus premium subscription When deviating from the plan feedback is unclear
Today, Zwift is launching Zwift Plus. This new premium tier pushes the monthly cost to $29.99, with a discounted yearly option at $299.99. In exchange for the upcharge, you unlock two core upgrades: real-world video routes and adaptive coaching.
Zwift considers this a massive milestone, which is why I recently went to Moab to celebrate the video-based routes ahead of launch. The concept was to ride the route indoors, then ride it outdoors to see how perfectly they matched. Unfortunately, we caught the tail end of a Pacific hurricane, so I only got to drive the route and ride it inside. Still, the big reveal ended up feeling almost anti-climactic—but in the best way possible.
The inside perfectly matches the real world, but you still get all the Zwift details you are used to. Zwift lays the graphics seamlessly into high-resolution and high frame rate footage. I rode the Tron bike in Arches National Park, and while it sadly doesn’t glow on the road, the wheels sit perfectly on the video road and the speed adjusts as you ride without ever breaking the illusion. It’s underwhelming, but only because it’s really good and feels like a natural extension of what Zwift already does. If you’ve used Rouvy, which Zwift now owns, this is better.
Personally, though, I don’t find the video-based routes all that much of a draw. They provide more variety, and that’s great, but Zwift already adds routes all the time and anyone who’s used Zwift knows the team is great at recreating real-life locations. What this launch is really all about is coaching, and that’s where the real magic is.
Part of why the team at Zwift considered this launch such a high-stakes proposition is that it’s a price increase, and that always comes with baggage. You could even consider the addition of the video routes to the Zwift Plus plan as a sort of tiered pricing structure where, all of a sudden, you have to pay for more routes. That’s not really true, but I can understand the hesitation.
I think part of why I don’t see that as an issue is because I don’t find the video routes to be the major news here. They are additional content, and as someone who will likely chew through every single additional badge Zwift offers this winter, that’s nice, but also not a big deal. Instead, I see this as a pretty clear value proposition of $10 a month for structured training.
With that in mind, my favorite thing about Zwift Plus is that I see it as a product that is going to consolidate the structured training market. I believe this will be a big hit to TrainerRoad, and I think that for many people, Zwift Plus will represent a net decrease in monthly subscriptions.
The reasons for this are pretty simple: structured training has to be good enough, and it has to create an environment where the user actually follows the plan. Before this launch, Zwift was mostly failing at both of those requirements.
Zwift already had training plans; they just weren’t engaging, they weren’t reactive, and they were widely considered to be not that great. With Zwift Plus, the first correction was the quality of the plans, and to address that, Zwift brought on Ryan Cooper.
If you aren’t familiar with the name, Ryan Cooper is the founder of Best Bike Split and the former Chief Scientist at TrainingPeaks. To understand why his involvement is so important, you have to look at what Best Bike Split actually does. It is a predictive physics engine that takes a rider’s specific power profile, weight, and aerodynamics, layers it over the exact elevation of a race course, and calculates exactly how many watts that rider should push on every single segment to finish as fast as possible without blowing up.
That is the level of data-driven modeling he brings to Zwift, and it is exactly why the brand is very careful to call this new coaching system “machine learning” rather than “AI.” Right now, AI is a marketing buzzword. When most people hear it, they picture a chatbot scraping the internet and hallucinating a generic training plan based on a text prompt.
Machine learning is different. It relies on math and datasets. In this case, Cooper’s algorithms were trained on the anonymized power and heart rate data of millions of Zwift riders, combined with peer-reviewed sports science. The system isn’t guessing or estimating based on what it read online. It uses actual machine learning to recognize patterns in your specific history, power data, and daily fatigue, and then mathematically calculates exactly what you need to do today to actually get faster.
This means Zwift has now solved the quality problem that TrainerRoad has so far always held as an advantage. But the raw quality of workouts is actually somewhat secondary in real life. You need not only quality workouts, but you need workouts that people will complete, and this is where Zwift has something no one else does.
Zwift controls everything about where you ride your bike, and that means the Zwift Plus workout plan has options. Once you set up your plan, the system will recommend an ever-changing variety in terms of how you complete a workout. My favorite example was actually the first day of the 12-week plan I started, when I was scheduled for a route rather than a set of intervals.
Except, if you squinted a bit, you’d see a clear interval workout. The route was the Watopia Mountain Route, and while it might appear to be a free ride, the route starts with a few miles of flats, then it climbs for a while before descending and finishing with some flats. What is actually happening there is that you get about 8-10 minutes of warm-up, then you have a work block of about 40 minutes before you get a rest, and finally a 20-ish minute cool-down where you ride the flats again. And Zwift knows, based on all your past rides both inside and out, exactly how hard you will ride each of those sections. Except I actually went harder because I started late and wanted to finish faster, so in my case, I got a notice asking if I wanted to adjust my plan based on the new intensity.
In the first week, I also had traditional intervals and a follow-the-RoboPacer session. The result is a tight training plan that adapts to you if you don’t follow it exactly, but rarely looks like a tight training plan. It’s a sort of trick to keep you engaged, and my money is on it working very well.
The only problem with this system is that, at launch, there’s not enough AI and there’s not enough feedback. I am told some of this will come, but it’s not super clear when or how much, so I have to evaluate what exists right now—and right now, it needs more interaction.
I am sure many people will not want to hear that this should have a chatbot, but I think it should. It has to be a good one, but for more than a year now I’ve bounced around between different AI systems, and when it works, it’s incredibly helpful. For a long time, I used Google Gemini paired with Garmin Connect, and this summer I’ve been playing with RideWithDave. Whatever system I’ve used, the main benefit is that you can ask the robot about deviations. “I have this scheduled; what if I do this instead? Does that fulfill the same goal?” Or, the opposite happens plenty, too: “Hey, I had this scheduled but instead I did this; did I satisfy the goal?” With the Zwift system, you just have to guess.
And once you do guess, there’s very little feedback one way or the other. One day, I had an interval session scheduled that was 2×20

articles.title_orig: Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
articles.title_zh: Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows Thomas Markle's son handing over VHS tapes and dismantled computers to police
Philippine police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex.
Earlier this month, it was reported that hundreds of images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle Sr, 82, had been found at the property in the Philippines.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr, who is now in the US, has strongly denied the allegations made by his son, describing them as "sick lies".
Cebu Regional Prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that Thomas Markle Jr was "adamant" that the case should be investigated, and that he felt his father "has to answer for it".
Last week, the Sun on Sunday reported that Thomas Markle Sr's ex-wife, Roslyn Loveless, had sent a letter to the Metropolitan Police about the 2019 allegations, which was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.
Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's two half-siblings. She divorced Thomas Markle Sr. in 1975, before he married the duchess's mother.
Thomas Markle Sr strongly denies the allegations of possessing images of child sexual abuse
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
Speaking to the Sun, Thomas Markle Jr also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".
Thomas Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May.
He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
The police say they must identify how the material was obtained before they can consider any criminal charges.
Campaigners describe Cebu as a known hotspot for the sexual exploitation of children, and authorities say they take any such allegations very seriously.

Update (11:23 AM ET): Nintendo announced a restock at the Nintendo Store , though it seems to be flashing in and out of stock. We were able to add it our basket after a few tries.

🚨 We’re tracking Zelda Switch 2 stock updates. If you’d like to know when more stock arrives, follow Matt Swider on X and turn on notifications. You can also become a free or paid subscriber to The Shortcut to help support our work. 🚨
A new update has dashed our hopes of a major Walmart restock of the Zelda Switch 2 console, which we were confident would happen today. However, a new Reddit post (thanks, Wario64 ) has revealed that Walmart is waiting until at least November 6 to sell the special edition console online.
🚨 Want the Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2? Drop your email for restock alerts before it sells out. ⤵️
A employee note says: “Due to a supply chain delay, some stores may not receive the Nintendo Switch 2 Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition in time for its planned Oct. 29 release. To allow time to fulfill preorders and reshop inventory as needed, the point-of-sale (POS) block will remain in place through at least Friday, Nov. 6. As inventory arrives, orders will be fulfilled based on preorder priority and available inventory.”
The Redditor who posted the news shared that some people were able to get the console from Walmart after 8:00am local time, so there is still hope.
Target recently updated its Zelda Switch 2 listing to reveal that it will also start taking orders of on November 6, with in stores orders beginning November 5. Clearly, the supply chain delay is impacting other stores, otherwise we likely would have seen a restock take place today, as we initially predicted.
We now know that Walmart and Target will be taking online orders, and that Best Buy and Nintendo are holding in-store events on November 5. GameStop is also letting customers pre-order in-store via their website .
Despite the news, we’ll still be tracking every retailer with our restock tracker, which provides up-to-the-second information whether something is in stock. If the Zelda Switch 2 does appear – which it might – our followers will still be one of the first to know.

articles.title_orig: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.title_zh: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
articles.content_orig:
South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.
The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.
It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.
South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.
The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.
For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.
South West Water performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents [BBC]
Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.
The Environment Agency's report card comes a month after South West Water was fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.
In the last year it also recorded the sharpest rise in customer complaints of any water company .
Serious incidents in the past year include pollution in St Austell River , killing thousands of fish, while pollution at Exmouth meant beachgoers had to leave the water .
Industry regulator Ofwat said the company met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".
It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.
Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.
While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.
It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.
A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.
"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."
They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".
"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.
"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."
People were advised against bathing at Exmouth after a pollution incident last year [BBC]
A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".
It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".
However, it said overall environmental performance "is poor".
In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".
To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.
Surfers Against Sewage described the latest performance ratings as "another league of shame for water companies" but she added they were "a mere slap on the wrist that means absolutely nothing".
Head of campaigns Jo Morley said: "What is the point in these environmental performance ratings when year after year water company behaviour gets worse?"

articles.title_orig: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Mongolian mining company says copper exports have dropped due to China border restrictions - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines says its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing
ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- The operator of one of Mongolia’s largest copper mines said Thursday its exports of copper concentrate to China have dropped by about 70% in the past two weeks due to restrictions at a border crossing.
The restrictions have raised concerns over potential revenue losses and disruptions to Mongolia’s massive mineral sector.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC, which operates Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world’s largest copper mines, said the number of truck convoys transporting copper concentrate across the Chinese border has fallen from the usual 12 to 13 per day to just around four. The restrictions affect vehicles crossing at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port, which is adjacent to Mongolia’s Gashuunsukhait Border Port.
The export cuts amount to a decline of about $300 million compared to normal operating conditions and could reach $1.2 billion if restrictions continue through the end of the year, local media reported on Wednesday.
Oyu Tolgoi LLC did not confirm the reported losses in a statement to The Associated Press on Thursday.
Mongolia is a major supplier of coal and copper to China, the world’s largest consumer of both commodities.
Mongolian border officials said the slowdown was related to infrastructure and technology upgrades at China’s Ganqimaodu Border Port.
Authorities in China’s Inner Mongolia region did not immediately answer questions from the AP.
In August, Chinese authorities introduced an in-vehicle facial recognition system for truck drivers crossing the border, and installation and maintenance work have affected border processing capacity, according to the Mongolian border authorities.
Mongolia’s government said the Chinese embassy in Ulaanbaatar informed it that the work, originally due to end by late September according to Mongolian news reports, may continue until the end of December.
Mongolian Finance Minister Mendsaikhan Zagdjav said some ministers were instructed during a Cabinet meeting to visit the border crossing and meet with Chinese authorities, according to local news reports.
All transport routes on the Mongolian side remain open and the government was not aware of any political reasons behind the restrictions, said the minister of Road and Transport, Delgersaikhan Borkhuu.
Mongolia’s copper sector has become an increasingly important contributor to national export revenues. During the first nine months of 2026, copper concentrate exports reportedly reached 2 million tons.
The border crossing restrictions have also affected Mongolia’s coal exports through Gashuunsukhait, with the number of vehicles crossing falling to just over 1,000 a day from 1,300 a day, border authorities said.
Mongolia has abundant mineral resources, including coal, copper, gold, uranium and fluorspar, and its economy relies heavily on mining, which accounts for roughly a quarter of its GDP. It is particularly sensitive to disruptions to cross-border trade and fluctuations in commodity prices.
Last year, coal and copper concentrates together accounted for 82.3% of Mongolia’s merchandise exports, while 89.4% of total exports went to China. Mongolia was also China’s leading supplier of imported coking coal, accounting for approximately 51% of Chinese coking coal imports in 2025.

articles.title_orig: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.title_zh: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.content_orig:
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

articles.title_orig: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.title_zh: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.title_zh: SpaceX stock slides back toward $140 as smaller space names leave it behind
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX took its worst one-day hit last Thursday since early August, when its biggest share unlock yet freed up to 1.3 billion shares to trade. Roughly a week later, it's back at the same floor, and the rest of the space trade has left it behind.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) shares slipped again on Thursday during premarket trading, along with nearly every space stock.
$140 has been SpaceX's floor since the summer. It marked the top of the stock's August trading range before a breakout, and it sits about halfway between the August low near $108 and the $172 ceiling that capped rallies in June and October.
That makes $140 support , a price where buyers have repeatedly stepped in. They did it twice this month, and the stock is back there again.
SpaceX fell about 9% on Oct. 22 as those shares unlocked.
Since then, the smaller names have done the running. Rocket Lab ( RKLB ), Firefly Aerospace ( FLY ), Intuitive Machines ( LUNR ) and AST SpaceMobile ( ASTS ) gained roughly 8% to 14% from the Oct. 22 close through Tuesday, while SpaceX barely budged.
That bounce followed a much rougher month for the group: over the past 30 days, those four are down roughly 20% to 35%, compared with a loss of about 3% for SpaceX.
The pullback comes as investors gear up for Anthropic's IPO, the next mega-listing, with JPMorgan again set to lead retail share sales as it did for SpaceX. SpaceX sits about a third below its June record close near $212.
A sustained break below $140 would open the door to a deeper slide toward the August low near $108. To turn the chart around, bulls first need to get back above the 50-day moving average, near $150, before taking another run at $172.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) report after the bell. How much more they plan to spend building AI data centers is the number most likely to move a stock that's now mostly an AI company .

articles.title_orig: Hello Kitty firm apologises, scraps Japan TV tie-up after China anger
articles.title_zh: Hello Kitty firm apologises, scraps Japan TV tie-up after China anger
articles.content_orig:
The company best known for its cute characters cut ties with the drama after strong Chinese criticism of its evocation of wartime torture
In an official statement released on its Japanese website on Thursday, the company acknowledged that the Japanese spy drama contained content that “does not align with the Sanrio Group’s corporate philosophy”.
The controversial series includes scenes depicting Chinese intelligence agents torturing Japanese operatives, prompting China’s state broadcaster CCTV to accuse the show of distorting history and “deliberately smearing” Beijing.
In its statement, Sanrio confirmed that it was ceasing the current collaboration with Vivant – which premiered in 2023 and opened its second season in July – along with all related future projects and promotional campaigns.

A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
articles.title_zh: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
articles.content_orig:
A first-time mum was denied hospital meals while her baby was "fighting for her life" because she was not breastfeeding.
Sophie Price, 22, was "shocked" when staff refused to give her a meal while her daughter Florence was being treated on a paediatric ward at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen.
Despite giving birth in the hospital five days earlier, she was told she was no longer classed as a patient as she was not breastfeeding, so she would not be provided with meals.
Aneurin Bevan health board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and was "committed to supporting families throughout their child's stay".
"It was just an awful experience. I just needed a hot meal to keep going for my daughter," said Sophie, from Newport.
Her family said they spent more than £1,000 on food from the canteen and takeaway meals during their three-week stay at the hospital while Florence was treated.
The health board said mothers are provided with meals while under the care of hospital maternity services as both them and their baby are classed as patients, whether they are breastfeeding or not.
But on paediatric wards, only the child is classed as the patient, however the hospital's policy is to provide breastfeeding mums with meals as this directly supports the baby's feeding and nutrition.
For babies who are formula-fed, the health board said formula was "provided as needed" by the hospital, but Sophie said she was told she would need to bring it in herself.
Sophie had only left the hospital - which earlier this week denied online claims it was "dangerous" and "dreadful" - for 24 hours before she and her husband Ryli Price had to return when they realised Florence was not able to breathe and the "colour started to drain from her".
"Florence started to make some really harsh grunting sounds, it sounded like a death rattle coming from her chest up into her mouth," she said.
Sophie ran into the A&E department screaming "she's not breathing" and credited the quick response of medical staff who helped save her daughter's life.
Florence was diagnosed with bronchiolitis , rhinoviruses - which causes the common cold - and a blood infection, which meant her lungs could not operate on their own.
She was placed on a machine that pumped air into her lungs via a mask.
Sophie said despite being "hungry and exhausted" she was denied a meal while her daughter was "in intensive care fighting for her life".
"Imagine being in a hospital with your seriously ill baby on breathing support monitors, overwhelmed with worry, anxiety and stress, only to be told you aren't entitled to a meal because you're formula feeding instead of breastfeeding," she said.
Sophie said she was bleeding through her clothes and "in a lot of pain" as her hips had to be put back in place after being dislocated during childbirth.
She also had a build-up of fluid in her feet called oedema , adding: "My feet, they were the size of elephant trunks to the point where I couldn't even walk from the one corridor to the next."
Sophie said she and Ryli were told Florence may need to be induced into a coma at any point and it was "so touch-and-go the whole time".
At one point, Sophie said she realised she had not eaten for about 28 hours and remembered seeing a food trolley being brought round to mums on the ward.
She said: "I remember them saying to me 'oh hi mum, hope you're OK, are you hungry?' And me saying 'oh yeah, I'm absolutely starving, I haven't eaten in ages. What have you got'?'"
Sophie was asked if she was breastfeeding, which she had not been able to do after the first 24 hours of Florence's life as she was no longer taking to her breast milk.
She explained this to staff and said Florence was being given formula, only to be told she was not able to have any food,
"I remember just being so shocked. It was so horrific," Sophie said, adding she already felt "disappointed" at being unable to breastfeed.
Due to her husband's paternity leave coming to an end, Sophie said she had "never been in such a vulnerable situation" and relied on family members to finish work and bring her food while she stayed at Florence's bedside.
Sophie's mother contacted the hospital about the issue, so it continued providing formula for Florence.
Sophie called the policy "outdated" and said it discriminated against formula-feeding mothers "who are doing their very best in difficult circumstances".
She thinks all hospitals should provide meals for mothers, regardless of how they are feeding their babies.
The health board thanked Sophie for her feedback and said it understood "how difficult and stressful it can be for parents when their child is in hospital".
It added: "Where parents are unable to access the hospital canteen, have limited support, or are unable to leave their child's bedside, ward teams can provide a selection of basic food items and refreshments to help meet immediate needs.
"Parents can also access a discounted hospital meal through a ward voucher scheme and where a family is experiencing financial hardship, support can be discussed with the ward team.
"Requests are considered on a case-by-case basis to ensure help is provided fairly and appropriately, taking account of the family's circumstances and the needs of the child."

articles.title_orig: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
articles.title_zh: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
articles.content_orig:
Parents and teenagers across Northern Ireland could face significant changes to how they access social media next year, with photo identification, banking information and facial scans among the methods identified to enforce the UK Government’s planned ban for under-16s.
Communications regulator Ofcom has identified four methods capable of providing highly effective age checks, as ministers prepare to publish detailed rules before the end of 2026.
The restrictions are expected to come into force in 2027, although the Government has yet to finalise precisely how the ban will operate, which services it will cover and how users will be required to prove their age.
The proposals could affect families throughout the UK, including Ballymena and the wider Mid and East Antrim area, with many adults also potentially facing additional checks before accessing social media platforms.
Ofcom's assessment identifies four approaches currently capable of reliably establishing whether someone is aged 16 or over.
• Photo ID matching – users provide a passport, driving licence or other accepted photo identification, which is checked against a live image of their face.
• Banking-based checks – with the user's consent, platforms access age information already held by a bank or financial institution.
• Digital ID services – users verify their identity through a digital service, potentially allowing them to confirm their age repeatedly without presenting identification each time.
• Facial age estimation – technology analyses facial features to estimate a person's age, with additional verification where the result is uncertain.
These are methods identified by the regulator, rather than a final list of checks that every platform will be required to offer.
Ofcom says facial age estimation technology can be inaccurate by several years around the age of 16. It therefore recommends a system similar to the Challenge 25 approach used by retailers selling alcohol.
Under this approach, platforms would set a higher age threshold for facial estimation and require further verification where a user appears close to the minimum permitted age.
One of the challenges identified by Ofcom is that some 16- and 17-year-olds do not currently hold the identification they may need to prove they are old enough to access restricted services.
The regulator estimates that approximately 94% of people aged 16 and over in the UK hold either a passport or driving licence. However, evidence suggests around 150,000 teenagers aged 16 and 17 have neither document.
Around 90% of UK teenagers in that age group are estimated to have a bank account, potentially providing another route to age verification.
Ofcom acknowledges that some young people may need to obtain identification to access social media once the restrictions are introduced.
Options include applying for a passport, provisional driving licence or a photo identification card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme (PASS). Some PASS cards are available free to 16- and 17-year-olds, including options that do not require existing photo identification.
Although the proposed ban is aimed at children under 16, its introduction could affect adult social media users.
Ofcom says platforms may not need to carry out fresh checks where they already hold accurate and reliable information establishing that an existing account holder is above the required age.
However, many adults are still likely to be asked to verify their age, using methods available under the regulator's existing guidance for age assurance at 18.
The assessment also raises questions about privacy, particularly where checks involve facial images, identity documents or financial information.
Ofcom says the available methods can be implemented in ways that protect personal information and comply with data protection legislation. It will continue working with the Information Commissioner's Office on these issues.
The regulator acknowledges that even highly effective age verification cannot prevent every underage user from accessing restricted platforms.
It says social media companies will need to take additional measures to identify and prevent attempts to circumvent the restrictions.
These could include making it easier for users to report suspected underage accounts and using technology to identify accounts that may belong to children who have bypassed the initial checks.
Ofcom says analysing users' online behaviour cannot replace an age check at registration because it requires someone to have already accessed the platform. However, such technology could help identify underage users afterwards.
Dame Melanie Dawes, Ofcom's Chief Executive , said:
“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right. It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply.
“We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play.”
Ofcom intends to publish research examining how children circumvent the restrictions within 12 months of the ban coming into effect.
A separate Ofcom report has also raised concerns about how app stores establish children's ages.
The regulator found that three-quarters of children who use the internet reported that apps downloaded from an app store were their primary means of going online.
However, all the app stores examined currently rely on children declaring their own age, with only limited additional verification in some circumstances.
Ofcom believes app stores could contribute to stronger online protections by introducing more reliable age checks, alongside better information about the risks individual apps pose to children.
App stores are not currently regulated under the Online Safety Act, and any decision to bring them within a future regulatory framework would be a matter for Government.
The regulator also suggests that protections operating across apps, devices and operating systems could be more effective than relying on individual social media platforms alone.
The Government announced its intention to introduce a ban for under-16s in June, drawing on Australia's approach while proposing stronger requirements for age verification.
Ministers intend to publish the first regulations before the end of this year, after which Ofcom will consult on detailed guidance for social media companies.
The regulator says it will be ready to take enforcement action against companies that fail to comply when the restrictions take effect in 2027.
For parents and young people in Northern Ireland, the key outstanding questions are which platforms will be covered, how existing accounts will be handled and what identification users will actually need. Those answers will depend on the final regulations, which have yet to be published.

articles.title_orig: China-Japan flights lose nearly 700,000 seats amid political spat
articles.title_zh: China-Japan flights lose nearly 700,000 seats amid political spat
articles.content_orig:
Chinese airlines cut back the most as tensions that began almost a year ago continue to depress tourism
Airlines will cut nearly 700,000 seats from their China-Japan flights and axe more than 5,000 flights for the coming winter travel season as a nearly year-old political squabble continues to depress tourism, according to aviation data provider OAG.
During the commercial aviation industry’s winter season, October 25 through March 27, carriers allocated a combined 2,871,270 seats, compared with 3,554,167 in the same season last year, OAG data showed.
The same airlines allocated 3,889,781 seats in the six months just ended, representing a cut of more than 1 million compared with the coming winter. Summer is traditionally a busier time of year for airlines.

articles.title_orig: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
articles.title_zh: Digging Into China’s Overlooked World War I History
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Hundreds of World War I -era bombs, grenades and artillery shells have been uncovered by the melting of ice in Italy’s Dolomite mountains, the Italian army reports.
Weapons used by the Italian and Austrian armies during the bitterly fought White War in the region, were found in September after a period of sustained glacial ice melt.
The latest finds follow an even bigger tranche of ordnance discovered during the melting over the summer.
In a statement, Italian Army officials said: "As the ice retreats, history resurfaces - and with it, dangers from the past. More than a century later, the mountains continue to yield unexploded ordnance from the Great War."
It's expected that as climate change further melts the Dolomites glaciers , more of the White War's dangerous legacy will emerge.
The officials added: "These complex operations-carried out amidst melting glaciers, steep slopes, and high-altitude terrain-demand a high level of technical expertise and experience.
"Clearing these areas means eliminating hidden dangers and making the trails-frequented every year by mountaineers, hikers, and tourists-safer."
The "White War" was fought between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces in the freezing, rugged mountain terrain between 1915 and 1918. It included some of the most horrific conditions of the First World War, as troops dug into defensive positions and endured extreme cold amid snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
Hikers reported several sightings of unexploded bombs during the summer, mainly around Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley, in the eastern Trentino region.
The Italian army subsequently carried out searches across several high-altitude areas of Trentino-Alto Adige, where retreating glaciers and melting snow have exposed wartime explosives.
Recent operations have focused on the Care Alto and Vedretta di Lares areas of the Adamello-Brenta region in Trento, as well as Val Martello and the Stelvio area in Bolzano.
The army said munitions had also been found at Cima Tre Cannoni and along the edges of the Livrio glacier.
The army said the work aimed to make mountain environments safer for mountaineers, hikers and tourists.
The White War was fought at high altitude, where troops endured extreme cold and faced the challenges of snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
More than a century later, the retreat of glaciers is exposing remnants of the conflict, including unexploded ordnance that can pose a danger to people exploring the mountains.
The army said the risks were not always immediately visible and tended to increase with altitude.
Its campaign to locate and neutralise unexploded munitions in the region is continuing as melting ice reveals further wartime remains.

articles.title_orig: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.title_zh: Chinese boy who donated US$1.5 to end power cuts now works for energy company
articles.content_orig:
Feeling that his first contribution was far too small for such a massive undertaking, Wang quietly made a second US$1.5 donation shortly after
A boy in central China who donated 10 yuan (US$1.5) to the Three Gorges Dam project in the 1990s now works for the power grid, helping transmit the electricity it generates across the country.
Wang Yu, 47, works for the State Grid Corporation of China in his hometown of Zigui county, Hubei province, according to Hubei Daily.
In 1991, 12-year-old Wang received a daily allowance of just one yuan – barely enough to buy breakfast – at a time when his parents earned a combined monthly salary of less than 100 yuan (US$15).

articles.title_orig: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
articles.title_zh: US should spy on Chinese firms to maintain edge in tech race: ex-CIA official
articles.content_orig:
Former CIA deputy director’s call to repeal Obama-era ban on economic espionage comes as Beijing rushes to protect trade secrets
A former CIA official has called for Washington to spy on foreign companies to help US firms stay ahead in the technology race, in what would represent a break from long-standing US policy amid intensifying competition with China.
“The US lead in many crucial advanced technologies is being contested or even erased by China,” wrote David Cohen, who served as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency under Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, in an article published by Foreign Affairs earlier this month.
“By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.”
